title: What 'proving it works' really means
idea: MEET. A solution isn't done when it runs — it's done when you've CHECKED it against examples you worked out yourself. Thinking, not typing.

exercises.prompt: You wrote a program and it runs with no error. Is it definitely correct?
exercises.explanation: Running is not the same as correct. A wrong plan runs fine and still gives a wrong answer. You must check the output.
options: No — running without errors doesn't prove the answer is right
Yes — no error means it's correct
Yes — the computer wouldn't run a wrong program
Only if it's short

exercises.prompt: What is the best EVIDENCE that a solution is correct?
exercises.explanation: A hand-worked example gives you the right answer in advance; matching it is real evidence the code is right.
options: Its output matches an example you worked out by hand
It looks tidy
It was quick to write
It has many lines

exercises.prompt: 'Proving it works' means trying ONE example and stopping there.
exercises.explanation: One example is a start, but you also test edge cases (empty, boundary, repeats). One happy example can hide bugs.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning in checking.
exercises.explanation: Checking has its own vocabulary: an example is a known input-output pair; an edge case is a tricky boundary; a verdict is pass or fail.

pairs.right: A known input and its correct output
A tricky input like empty or a boundary

exercises.prompt: Why work the example out BY HAND before running the code?
exercises.explanation: If you compute the answer after seeing the code's output, you'll just trust the code. Hand-first gives an independent check.
options: So you have an independent answer to compare against
Because hands are faster than computers
So you can skip running the code
Because the computer can't do math

exercises.prompt: If the output does NOT match your hand example, the first suspect is your plan/code, not your hand example.
exercises.explanation: Usually the code is wrong — but check your hand math too. The point is the mismatch tells you to investigate.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps of proving a solution works.
exercises.explanation: Pick inputs, work the right answer by hand, run the code, compare. Comparison is the whole point of checking.
blocks: Work out its correct output by hand
Run the code on that input
Compare the output to your hand answer

exercises.prompt: A classmate says 'it printed a number, so it works.' What's missing from their reasoning?
exercises.explanation: Printing a number only shows it ran. They never compared it to a known-correct answer, so they proved nothing.
options: They never compared the number to a known-correct answer
Nothing — that's enough
They should print two numbers
They should make it longer

exercises.prompt: Which is a THINKING skill this unit builds?
exercises.explanation: This unit is about reasoning: choosing good test inputs and judging pass/fail. That is verification thinking, not typing.
options: Choosing good test inputs and judging pass or fail
Typing faster
Memorising syntax
Writing longer programs

exercises.prompt: Checking is the LAST step of UEPCC, and it is often the hardest.
exercises.explanation: Yes — Check is last and hardest because it needs honesty: you must try to break your own solution, not just admire it.
